app_rules: Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.

No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.

The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.

Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

rules: Infer the likely audience, competing alternatives, platform expectations, and risky unknowns from the prompt.
If facts are uncertain, label them as assumptions rather than pretending external research was performed.
Decide what would make the app feel native and valuable on iPhone, not just technically possible.
Every factual claim cites its source (URL from the prompt's fetched context, or is marked ASSUMPTION).
Include a concrete competitor comparison (names, what they do well, the gap this app exploits).
required_output: Comparable apps or patterns to learn from.
acceptance_checks: The next phase can use the output without repeating discovery.
At least three concrete risks or unknowns are named.
The research points toward a shippable first version.
No unsourced factual claims — each is cited or explicitly marked ASSUMPTION.

rules: Name a design language for THIS app (e.g. 'warm paper journal', 'precision instrument dark') with a one-line rationale; 'clean and modern' is a rejection-worthy non-answer.
State the emotional target: how the user should feel on the main screen, in one sentence.
Pick one signature interaction (a hero moment of motion, layout, or feedback) that expresses the design language.
Describe the default-looking version of this app (plain List, stock chrome, system accent) and explicitly reject it, naming at least three concrete differences.
Design real screens and states, not vague UX language.
Make navigation, empty states, errors, onboarding, and persistence visible.
Use iOS-native patterns unless the prompt clearly demands otherwise.
required_output: Rejected default option and the concrete differences from it.
acceptance_checks: The design language is specific to this app; swapping in a different app's name would make it wrong.
The default-looking option is explicitly rejected with named differences, not just adjectives.
A SwiftUI developer can create the view hierarchy from this output.
Every required user workflow has a screen/state path.

rules: Emit a structured DESIGN SPEC under fixed headings (Type Scale, Spacing, Colors, Corner Radii, Components, Navigation, Screen States, Motion & Haptics, Accessibility) that the build phase consumes verbatim.
Give explicit values everywhere: point sizes and weights, spacing steps, corner radii, and light AND dark color hex values; no adjective may stand in for a number.
Carry design_discussion's named design language and signature interaction into concrete named components.
Every primary screen must include layout intent, key components, state variants (loading/empty/error/populated), accessibility, and motion guidance.
If external Claude Design is desired, provide a clean prompt/upload plan the user can use directly.
required_output: DESIGN SPEC - Type scale: every text role with explicit size/weight (e.g. Title 28 semibold) mapped to a Dynamic Type style.
DESIGN SPEC - Spacing grid: base unit (4 or 8pt) and the named steps used for padding and gaps.
DESIGN SPEC - Semantic color palette: named roles (background, surface, text primary/secondary, accent, success/warning/error) each with a light and a dark hex value.
DESIGN SPEC - Corner radii: named steps (e.g. small/medium/large) with point values.
DESIGN SPEC - Component inventory: every screen's components named (e.g. StatCard, StreakRing, EntryRow), mapped to the screens that use each one.
DESIGN SPEC - Navigation pattern: the tab/stack/sheet map for the whole app.
DESIGN SPEC - Per-screen empty, loading, and error states with copy, icon, and recovery action.
DESIGN SPEC - Motion and haptics notes: which transitions animate, with what curve, and which events fire feedback.
DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility: Dynamic Type behavior, contrast expectations, VoiceOver labels for icon-only controls.
Claude Design prompt or explicit no-external-design decision.
acceptance_checks: A SwiftUI builder can write Theme.swift (fonts, spacing, colors, radii) directly from the spec with zero invented values.
Every screen has named components and defined empty/loading/error states — not just the happy path.
Every color role has both a light and a dark hex value.
The handoff does not depend on hidden design decisions.
The design direction is premium and category-specific.

rules: Review the product through iOS-specific constraints before tech_specs locks implementation.
Prefer SwiftUI, Apple frameworks, local persistence, and permissive dependencies only.
Call out privacy, permissions, offline behavior, StoreKit, ML/AR feasibility, and testability.
acceptance_checks: The app can be built as a native iOS app without vague architecture gaps.
Any ML, LLM, or AR use is justified by user value.
No dependency violates the permissive-license policy.

rules: Choose the simplest architecture that supports the MVP and tests.
Specify data models, services, persistence, concurrency boundaries, and error handling.
Prefer Apple frameworks and permissive dependencies only.
Emit the required interfaces-json block.
The Red Team's job here: name at least one requirement or edge case the spec missed before closing.
acceptance_checks: Parallel build lanes can work without inventing incompatible types.
The spec names how the app will be built and verified.

rules: Act as the final pre-build gate, not another planning brainstorm.
Check consistency across prompt contract, product brief, design handoff, iOS architecture, tech specs, project plan, and tasks.
Resolve contradictions by downgrading scope or naming a blocker before code starts.
acceptance_checks: The build phase can start without inventing product/design/architecture decisions.
Every major workflow has an acceptance criterion.
Testing responsibilities are explicit.

rules: Build real files in app_build; do not only describe the solution.
Create the design spec's tokens as a single theme file (Theme.swift or equivalent) before building screens, and style every view through it; scattered font/spacing/color literals are defects.
Implement the handoff's named components, per-screen empty states, and dark-mode palette as specified; a default unstyled List where the spec says otherwise is a defect.

Every interactive element (buttons, cells, fields, toggles) must set .accessibilityIdentifier — the UI-crawl gate and declared flows target elements by it, and it doubles as accessibility support. When a DECLARED FLOW TOKENS contract is present, expose each of those tokens VERBATIM as the matching control's .accessibilityIdentifier (keep a descriptive .accessibilityLabel for VoiceOver — set BOTH); an independently-named identifier fails that journey.
Implement screens with ALL specified states: empty, loading, error, and populated. A screen with only the happy path is incomplete.
Keep changes scoped to the assigned lane and leave integration files to the integrator.
Every iteration should reduce compile, runtime, or product-completeness risk.
When generating iOS, include unit/UI test targets where feasible.
acceptance_checks: The app has a runnable entry point.
The main user workflow is implemented end-to-end.
A single theme/token file exists, views use it, dark mode works, and all specified states (empty/loading/error/populated) are real.
Interactive elements carry accessibilityIdentifiers (crawl/flow targetable).
Every declared-flow tap/type token is exposed as the exact .accessibilityIdentifier of the control that satisfies that step.
The integrator has wired lane outputs together.

rules: Cover every important workflow, not only the happy path.
Include simulator/device steps, expected results, and regression checks.
Include accessibility, persistence, permissions, offline behavior, and subscription/paywall checks when relevant.
acceptance_checks: A human can run the checklist without asking what to tap.
Every core feature from app_features appears in QA.
Failure states are tested, not ignored.

rules: Write REAL XCTest unit tests against the app_build code just written — never placeholder/empty tests that only assert true.
Prioritize coverage of core logic and view-models (business rules, data transforms, state machines) over trivial UI snapshot tests.
Add a dedicated test target/scheme if the project doesn't already have one, so xcodebuild -list can discover it (build_verification's xcodebuild test run depends on this).
Keep tests deterministic — no network calls, no real timers/sleeps, no reliance on wall-clock or external state.
Do not modify production code to make a test pass; fix the test or file a note if production code looks wrong.
required_output: Which test target/scheme was created or extended.
List of test files added and what each covers.
Any core logic left untested and why.
acceptance_checks: At least one real XCTestCase file exists under a discoverable test target.
Tests exercise actual app_build types/functions, not stubs.
No test hard-fails immediately from a missing import/target wiring mistake.

tech_stack._docs: Approved-library registry (task #4). Spliced into tech_specs/build context and enforced by designlint.py: 'banned' entries are lint ERRORS; when 'allowed' is non-empty, any other third-party SPM dependency is a WARNING (error in runtime.design_lint_strict). System frameworks (SwiftUI, SwiftData, Foundation, ...) are always fine and never need listing.

banned.name: Alamofire
banned.why: URLSession covers every need here; no third-party networking.

banned.name: SwiftyJSON
banned.why: Codable is the standard; unmaintained-style JSON wrappers add risk.

banned.name: realm
banned.why: SwiftData/GRDB are the approved persistence choices.

tech_stack.notes: Prefer system frameworks first: URLSession for networking, SwiftData for persistence, Swift Charts for charts, OSLog for logging. A new third-party dependency needs a one-line justification in tech_specs.

prototype: Every core feature in the prompt/requirements is FUNCTIONALLY implemented, not just visually present: real logic runs, real data is produced/stored, real state changes persist across navigation and relaunch where the feature implies it should.
The primary user workflow works end-to-end (create/see/act on the core object) using REAL data entered by the user, not hardcoded placeholder content standing in for it.
The app launches to a real screen, not a placeholder.
No crash on the primary workflow.
mvp: Every screen has empty, loading, and error states — not just the happy path.
Dark mode is styled (both palettes from the design handoff, readable).
Onboarding or a self-explanatory first screen exists.
All views style through DesignSystem tokens (no inline colors/fonts).
Every interactive element has an accessibilityIdentifier.
v1: All declared user flows (flows.json) pass against the built app.
No TODO/FIXME markers left in source.
Settings/preferences screen exists where the prompt implies configurability.
App icon and display name are set.
production_draft: Unit or UI test target exists and runs.
Accessibility audit issues addressed (labels, contrast, dynamic type).
No dead buttons (every tappable does something).

review_prompts.ios_architecture_review: Review the app specifically as a modern iOS product. Prefer SwiftUI, Apple frameworks, local persistence first, privacy by design, and permissive dependencies only. Call out permissions, entitlements, StoreKit/subscriptions, background work, ML/AR feasibility, and UI/unit test strategy before tech_specs locks the contracts.

contract_snippets.flows: MACHINE CONTRACT (required): ALSO emit ONE fenced ```flows-json``` block of the form {"flows": [{"name": "add first item", "steps": [{"tap": "home.addItemButton"}, {"type": "Sample", "into": "addEdit.nameField"}, {"tap": "addEdit.saveButton"}, {"assert_exists": "Sample"}, {"back": true}]}]}. Cover EVERY primary user journey the app promises (3-8 flows). Every tap/type step MUST name a stable dotted accessibilityIdentifier (screen.controlName) — PREFER accessibilityIdentifiers over visible labels: an identifier is a contract the build MUST honor, whereas a visible label drifts during the build. NEVER name a bare glyph or symbol as a tap/type token ('+', 'x', '×', '°F', a gear icon): an icon-only control has no matchable text, so reference it by its accessibilityIdentifier — or, if you must use a label, name the EXACT full accessibilityLabel the control will expose ('Add custom tea'), never the glyph. assert_exists MAY instead name a user-visible string you expect on screen (e.g. the item you just created). When an asserted state only arrives after an app-determined delay — a timer completing, a countdown reaching zero — add "timeout": <seconds> to THAT step (e.g. {"assert_exists": "Ready", "timeout": 95}), sized to the app's own duration plus margin: the default wait is ~5 seconds, so a timer's completion state can NEVER pass without a declared timeout. Route such flows through the SHORTEST built-in duration. Never route a flow through a control hidden behind a gesture (swipe actions, long-press context menus): the gate taps directly-visible controls only, so a journey needing edit/delete must use a visibly exposed affordance. Whatever a step names, the built app has to expose that EXACT string on the control or the UI-crawl gate fails the journey. These are executed against the real built app by the UI-crawl gate — a journey you forget to declare is a journey nobody verifies.
